{"id": "88:21/q01", "question": "How does the opening fā connect the command to what precedes it?", "turns_on": "Whether the consequence is drawn from the preceding proofs and refusal to reflect or from God's lordship and coming judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q01/p1", "position": "After the signs and the account of resurrection, the Messenger must remind people even when they fail or refuse to reflect.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and his full version point to proofs of oneness and resurrection; Biqāʿī points to creation's proof of power, Paradise and Hell, and innate recognition; Ibn al-Zubayr, reported by Biqāʿī, traces the damned, blessed, created signs, then reminder. Al-Kashshāf, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī, Elmali̇li, and Ibn ʿĀshūr emphasize their failure or refusal to reflect; Ibn ʿĀshūr also connects the order to rejection of resurrection."}, {"id": "88:21/q01/p2", "position": "The command follows from God's sole lordship and the judgment awaiting believers and unbelievers.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī gives these as the reason to remind without coercing."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q02", "question": "What does the command to remind call the Messenger to communicate?", "turns_on": "Whether 'remind' is glossed as preaching, recalling favors and duties, presenting proofs, or conveying revelation; several notes combine these contents.", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q02/p1", "position": "He should preach, admonish and warn people.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies Mecca and comparison with earlier prophets. Al-Māwardī and his full version give preaching as one interpretation; Ibn ʿAbbās as reported by al-Wāḥidī and Ibn al-Jawzī describe admonition at that stage. Al-Qurṭubī and his full version say admonish and warn. Al-Dāmghānī gives dhikr the sense of admonition or exhortation with the Qurʾān. Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, Elmali̇li and Corpus Coranicum also speak of preaching or warning."}, {"id": "88:21/q02/p2", "position": "He should explain divine proofs and signs, especially oneness, resurrection and the need to reflect.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās supplies God's proofs and signs as the understood object; al-Wāḥidī includes proofs of oneness. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this verse and like signs; al-Ṭabrisī reports al-Jubbāʾī and Abū Muslim urging reasoning from these proofs. Al-Rāzī adds resurrection and warning against neglect; al-Nasafī says the proofs invite reflection. Biqāʿī invokes creation and innate knowledge of divine power; Quṭb names the afterlife and creation signs."}, {"id": "88:21/q02/p3", "position": "He should recall God's favors and people's duties so they respond with fear, gratitude and worship.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī gives signs, proofs, favors, duties and admonition; his full version stresses favors and obligations. Al-Māwardī and his full version say recalling blessings brings fear of punishment. Al-Wāḥidī includes blessings with proofs of oneness; al-Ṭabrisī says reminder makes the favor and duty intelligible and calls for gratitude and worship."}, {"id": "88:21/q02/p4", "position": "He should convey the revelation and what he was sent with.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr and the parallel note on the next verse say to remind people of what was sent with him. Al-Kashshāf cites 42:48 for the duty of conveying; Quṭb names the afterlife and creation signs; Kuranyolu specifies conveying revelation."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q03", "question": "Whom is the Messenger told to remind?", "turns_on": "Whether the addressees are unrestricted, narrowed by capacity to benefit, specified as Meccans or the elect, or limited by attachment of the following exception.", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q03/p1", "position": "People or God's servants generally.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls them God's servants; al-Naḥḥās says the omitted object is God's servants. Al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, and Kuranyolu describe the people addressed by preaching or warning. Al-Māwardī likewise says 'them' without restricting the audience."}, {"id": "88:21/q03/p2", "position": "Anyone who might benefit or is prepared to rise toward God.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī and his full version say to awaken innate knowledge in anyone likely to benefit. Al-Qāshānī says reminder can benefit a soul prepared to ascend; he contrasts the veiled person who turns away and faces the great fire, understood as absolute veiling across all levels of existence."}, {"id": "88:21/q03/p3", "position": "The people of Mecca.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies Mecca's people, comparing the Prophet's warning with earlier prophets."}, {"id": "88:21/q03/p4", "position": "Discerning believers, especially the elect.", "reasons": "Abū al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAṭāʾ, reported by al-Sulamī, distinguishes admonition for ordinary people, counsel for brethren and reminder for the elect; reminder to discerning believers remains obligatory lest the Sunnah and obligations lapse."}, {"id": "88:21/q03/p5", "position": "The people, except those who turn away and cannot benefit.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports this as an alternative syntactic attachment of the later exception to 'remind'."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q04", "question": "Why is the object of 'remind' unspoken?", "turns_on": "Whether the missing object is recovered from shared knowledge of the signs or from the following clause.", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q04/p1", "position": "The hearer already knows the object: God's servants are to be reminded of His signs and proofs.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās explicitly explains the omission through what is already understood."}, {"id": "88:21/q04/p2", "position": "The following statement that he is no controller over them supplies the omitted object.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr and his full version connect the unexpressed object to the next verse, 88:22."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q05", "question": "Does the imperative call for sustained reminder?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q05/p1", "position": "Yes, he must keep reminding despite inattention and obstacles.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr and his full version read the imperative as continued effort. Al-Rāzī and his full version say the commission requires patient endurance of obstacles; Ibn ʿĀshūr links the continuation to refusal to listen."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q06", "question": "What response should reminder seek from hearers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q06/p1", "position": "They should reason from clear signs and act on what reflection teaches.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says explanation makes needed knowledge intelligible and that explicit religious proofs make blind imitation inadequate, linking 51:55 and 16:67; he reports al-Jubbāʾī and Abū Muslim urging inference from the proofs. Elmali̇li says reflection on creation leads to knowledge of divine ways, commands and useful deeds."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q07", "question": "What does 'you are only a reminder' limit or explain?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q07/p1", "position": "It confines the Messenger's mission to reminder and conveyance, without control over acceptance or blame for refusal, and explains why he should persist.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī says negation after innamā excludes a competing agent, whereas negation before it corrects the actor; the verse uses the former pattern, with 88:22. Al-Ālūsī says the clause explains the command. Ibn ʿĀshūr says its added restriction explains persistence despite inattention and removes responsibility for producing recollection. Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Nasafī compare 42:48 on conveyance; Quṭb cites 88:17–20. Al-Qāshānī calls the reminder and no-control clause an interruption and cites 28:56 and 50:45. Al-Study Quran cites 13:40, 3:20, 5:92, 5:99, 16:35, 16:82, 29:18, 36:17, 42:48 and 64:12."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q08", "question": "Can the Prophet compel belief or be held responsible when people do not respond?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q08/p1", "position": "He can deliver and warn, but cannot force faith, guarantee guidance, or bear blame for their refusal; guidance and reckoning belong to God.", "reasons": "Muqātil says he is no king over them; al-Qushayrī and al-Baghawī deny control or forced belief. Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say he need not be distressed or blamed for refusal. Ibn Kathīr assigns reckoning to God; al-Bursevī assigns guidance and success to God. Kuranyolu argues faith and worship require inward conviction and cites 3:20, 16:82, 28:56 and 42:48. Corpus Coranicum rejects reading the later exception as giving power over unbelievers because 88:21–22 deny compulsion."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q09", "question": "Was the no-compulsion directive superseded by permission to fight?", "turns_on": "Whether later fighting authorized compulsory belief or concerned harmful acts while faith still required free conviction.", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q09/p1", "position": "Yes; the reminder-only direction belonged to the period before fighting was commanded and was abrogated by the fighting verse.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says reminder was commanded before fighting. Ibn ʿAbbās as reported by al-Wāḥidī and Ibn al-Jawzī call the mission reminder-only at that time; Biqāʿī locates it in an early Meccan period of forbearance. Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī explicitly say the fighting verse abrogated the rule."}, {"id": "88:21/q09/p2", "position": "No; authorization to fight did not end the ban on forcing belief.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu rejects the abrogation claim: after fighting was allowed, the Prophet still did not force belief, and punitive action was directed at harmful agitators."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q10", "question": "What does the reported Prophetic statement say about fighting and the profession of faith?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q10/p1", "position": "The Prophet said he was ordered to fight until people profess God's oneness; then their lives and property are protected except by due right, and God handles their reckoning.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports Jābir's version with re

{"id": "88:21/q11", "question": "Who is addressed by the closing command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q11/p1", "position": "The Prophet Muhammad.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the address could be general, but internal evidence and the closing command to remind identify the Prophet. Corpus Coranicum observes the direct address to the Messenger. Numerous commentators name Muhammad or the Prophet as recipient."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q12", "question": "How do inward readings understand the practice and benefit of reminder?", "turns_on": "The inward notes emphasize different conditions: the hearer's rank, the preacher's authority and adaptation, or the soul's preparedness.", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q12/p1", "position": "Reminder especially addresses the elect and discerning believers, and must continue for them.", "reasons": "Abū al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAṭāʾ, reported by al-Sulamī, grades admonition for ordinary hearers, counsel for brethren and reminder for the elect; neglect would cause the Sunnah and obligations to lapse."}, {"id": "88:21/q12/p2", "position": "True preaching addresses each listener according to capacity and requires authority to counsel.", "reasons": "Al-Junayd, reported by al-Sulamī, describes luminous counsel, takes the Prophet as its model, and requires authorization for real preaching."}, {"id": "88:21/q12/p3", "position": "Reminder may help a soul prepared to ascend, while one veiled from the cause by its effects faces the great fire.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī defines that fire as punishment of absolute veiling through every level of existence."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q13", "question": "What inward correspondences does Biqāʿī draw from the earlier creation signs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q13/p1", "position": "The camel corresponds to tranquil souls, the sky to luminous spirits, mountains to firm intellects and knowledge, and earth to the body and its organs.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī offers these as inward counterparts to the created signs."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q14", "question": "How does the closing command fit the sūra and its neighboring sūras?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the command to different scopes: its own passage, neighboring sūras, or a broader pattern of direct address.", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q14/p1", "position": "It concludes a sequence of the damned, the blessed and created proofs that failed to persuade.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Zubayr, reported by Biqāʿī, says the passage follows divine transcendence and the magnification of resurrection, then moves through the damned's ordeal (88:6), the blessed, signs (88:17), and command (88:21)."}, {"id": "88:21/q14/p2", "position": "It completes the preceding sūra's call to purification and leads into the next sūra's lesson about time and the final return.", "reasons": "Elmali̇li says creation's signs disclose divine ways and useful deeds before the command; the next sūra draws attention to changes in time while explaining return to God."}, {"id": "88:21/q14/p3", "position": "Its direct address to the Prophet forms part of a developing sūra-ending pattern.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says earlier direct addresses occur only as short consolations in sūras 93, 94 and 108; in group II, such address enters broader literary settings and becomes a regular closing feature."}]}
{"id": "88:21/q15", "question": "What virtue is reported for reciting Sūrat al-Ghāshiya?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "88:21/q15/p1", "position": "Its reciter is promised an easy reckoning.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī's full version reports this from the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "88:22/q01", "question": "What does muṣayṭir mean?", "turns_on": "The sources choose different aspects of control: authority, tyranny, mastery, oversight, or conquest.", "positions": [{"id": "88:22/q01/p1", "position": "One who has authority, control, or dominance over others.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Ibn Qutayba, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī and others give power, control, or domination as the sense. Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites the Arabic idiom tasyṭara ʿalaynā fulān. Al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Kashshāf, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī and Corpus Coranicum compare 50:45; al-Rāzī also cites 10:99. Al-Rāghib, reported by Bursawī, likens it to standing over and maintaining something, with 13:33 and 6:107. Asad gives the literal sense as having power over them."}, {"id": "88:22/q01/p2", "position": "A tyrant or coercive ruler who subdues and compels people.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid repeatedly gloss it as a tyrant; Ibn ʿAbbās adds pardon and forbearance in Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Durr. Qatāda speaks of subduing or compelling. Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds arrogant domination. Al-Kashshāf and others compare the denial of tyranny in 50:45. The contextual force is coercive power, especially over faith."}, {"id": "88:22/q01/p3", "position": "A master, lord, or king over them.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan gives lord or master; Muqātil says the Prophet has no kingly authority; al-Kashshāf also says master."}, {"id": "88:22/q01/p4", "position": "An overseer or recorder who watches and keeps account.", "reasons": "Al-Ṣiḥāḥ as reported by al-Qurṭubī includes overseeing, tending affairs and recording deeds; Bursawī calls this monitoring, and al-Qummī negates the Prophet's being a keeper or scribe."}, {"id": "88:22/q01/p5", "position": "A conqueror over them.", "reasons": "Qatāda gives this gloss in both al-Durr versions."}]}
{"id": "88:22/q02", "question": "What is the derivation of muṣayṭir?", "turns_on": "Whether the proposed s-ṭ-r connection explains the word through writing, domination, or remains uncertain.", "positions": [{"id": "88:22/q02/p1", "position": "It derives from s-ṭ-r, writing or a bounded line.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Ṣiḥāḥ explain that a written line stays within bounds, and the overseer preserves matters in writing according to al-Jishumī. Al-Naḥḥās says sīn becomes ṣād before ṭāʾ; Bursawī likewise calls sīn original and ṣād assimilated for the following ṭāʾ. Corpus Coranicum attributes the writing link to Jeffery, while leaving the origin uncertain."}, {"id": "88:22/q02/p2", "position": "Its root expresses domination or overpowering.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says saṭara ʿalayhi means he dominated him, and describes original sīn replaced by ṣād. Al-Qurṭubī adds that saṭarahu can mean knocking someone down."}, {"id": "88:22/q02/p3", "position": "Its etymology is uncertain.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says the etymology is unclear even though Jeffery proposes s-ṭ-r, writing; it still accepts the contextual sense on comparison with 50:45."}]}
{"id": "88:22/q03", "question": "How is the form of muṣayṭir analyzed in Arabic?", "turns_on": "How many comparable Arabic forms count and whether the apparently similar names are diminutives.", "positions": [{"id": "88:22/q03/p1", "position": "It is a rare participial pattern shared with four named forms.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān list musayṭir, mubayṭir, mubayqir and muhaymin. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān suggest the names Mujaymir and Mudaybir could instead be diminutives. Abū Ḥayyān uses the verb sayṭara and its derivative or passive to support transitivity; al-Samīn says Hārūn's open-ṭāʾ form is a passive participle of this transitive verb."}, {"id": "88:22/q03/p2", "position": "Only muṣayṭir and mubayṭir exemplify this pattern.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports Abū ʿUbayda's two-word inventory."}, {"id": "88:22/q03/p3", "position": "The proposed diminutive analysis of similar names is unsound.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn questions treating Mujaymir and Mudaybir as diminutives, recalling his judgment that a diminutive analysis of muhaymin at 5:48 was a grave error."}]}
{"id": "88:22/q04", "question": "How is bi-muṣayṭir recited?", "turns_on": "The transmitted consonant and ṭāʾ vowel, with codex spelling, original sīn, neighboring ṭāʾ, dialect and route evidence.", "positions": [{"id": "88:22/q04/p1", "position": "With initial ṣād and kasra on ṭāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ notes that ṣād matches the written form and is valid; al-Nāshʾr details ṣād routes for Qunbul, Ibn Dhakwān, Ḥafṣ and Khallād, including split readings against 52:37. Ibn Mujāhid names Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and ʿĀṣim; al-Nasafī names Medinan and Basran readers, ʿAlī and ʿĀṣim. Jābir's ṣād recitation is reported as authenticated by al-Ḥākim. Al-Bursawī says the following ṭāʾ favors emphatic ṣād."}, {"id": "88:22/q04/p2", "position": "With initial sīn, its original consonant.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ contrasts recitation with the ṣād script. Routes vary: Ibn Mujāhid gives reports for Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Kisāʾī; Ibn al-Jawzī names Abū Razīn, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Qatāda and al-Ḥulwānī from Ibn ʿĀmir. Ibn al-Jazarī details Hishām, Qunbul, Ibn Dhakwān and Ḥafṣ, including routes where 52:37 differs. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Biqāʿī give al-Kisāʾī; Ibn ʿĀshūr gives Hishām. Qirāʾāt ER says meaning stays controller with less emphasis."}, {"id": "88:22/q04/p3", "position": "With an intermediate ṣād colored toward zāy.", "reasons": "Ḥamza's reading is reported by Ibn Mujāhid, al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr; al-Samīn distinguishes Khalaf and two Khallād routes. Ibn al-Jazarī says most eastern and western Khallād transmitters use this sound and know no contrary text, while another route gives ṣād. Qirāʾāt ER says the semantic shift is slight."}, {"id": "88:22/q04/p4", "position": "With fatḥa on ṭāʾ, an open vowel in Tamīm usage.", "reasons": "Hārūn or Hārūn al-Aʿwar transmits this dialect form. {"id": "88:22/q05", "question": "Whom does ʿalayhim restrict the denial of control to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "88:22/q05/p1", "position": "The people being addressed or warned, specifically these hearers.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the preposition marks domination and limits the denial to those people; he expects the Prophet to gain authority over others later. Muqātil identifies the hearers as Mecca's people. Corpus Coranicum calls them the Messenger's hearers."}]}
{"id": "88:22/q06", "question": "Why is ʿalayhim placed before bi-muṣayṭir?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "88:22/q06/p1", "position": "To preserve the verse ending and cadence.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the prepositional complement precedes its predicate for the rhyme or cadence."}]}
{"id": "88:22/q07", "question": "What task and limit does this statement give the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether the limit refers to the lasting inability to produce inward belief or also to a temporary prohibition of fighting and killing.", "positions": [{"id": "88:22/q07/p1", "position": "He must remind, warn, and convey; he cannot force belief or hearts, and the outcome and reckoning belong to God.", "reasons": "Muqātil compares earlier prophets and Mecca. Al-Ṭabarī says leave them to God's judgment; Qatāda says God's servants belong to Him. Ibn Zayd denies forcing people back into faith. Al-Rāzī cites 50:45 and 10:99; al-Ṭabrisī adds patient invitation, not forcing faith into hearts. Ibn Kathīr says his commission is to convey; al-Qushayrī calls reminder his entrusted mission. Elmalılı says he cannot compel reflection, thoughts or hearts, citing 28:56. Quṭb says hearts remain under God's power and the preacher is freed from carrying the outcome. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the statement reassurance that continued disbelief is not his responsibility. Kur'an Yolu says faith and worship need inward conviction, citing 3:20, 16:82, 28:56 and 42:48; Study Quran lists 13:40, 3:20, 5:92, 5:99, 16:35, 16:82, 29:18, 36:17, 42:48 and 64:12. Corpus Coranicum also compares reminders in 51:55, 80:3-4 and 87:9-10."}, {"id": "88:22/q07/p2", "position": "He was then barred from killing or coercing the rejecters.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī explicitly give a pre-fighting limit on killing as well as coercion, usually as the rule later abrogated. Al-Rāzī reports the same account of the commentators."}]}
{"id": "88:22/q08", "question": "How does the clause relate to the preceding command to remind?", "turns_on": "Whether the explanatory clause is described as apposition or interruption.", "positions": [{"id": "88:22/q08/p1", "position": "It restates and explains the restriction: the Prophet's charge is reminder, not control.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it an appositive elaboration of the preceding restriction's negative side; the command is to persist in reminder, and its omitted object is supplied by this clause. Innamā explains why he must continue despite inattention and reassures him that acceptance is not his charge. Al-Ālūsī says the clause confirms the warning's limit; al-Qushayrī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī also make it the explanation of his mission."}, {"id": "88:22/q08/p2", "position": "It is an interrupting clause within the surrounding reminder and punishment passage.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī explicitly calls the reminder and non-control clause an interruption and cites 28:56 and 50:45."}]}
{"id": "88:22/q09", "question": "Was the denial of control abrogated by fighting commands?", "turns_on": "Whether the negation concerned a historical ban on fighting or the continuing inability to cause faith, and how later fighting is understood.", "positions": [{"id": "88:22/q09/p1", "position": "Yes, the earlier restraint was abrogated by the fighting or sword verse.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī hold this; al-Rāzī attributes it to the commentators. Ibn Zayd cites 9:73 and 9:5 but says the duty of reminder in 51:55 remains; Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Naḥḥās's reported view specify killing polytheists wherever found at 9:5. Al-Wāḥidī describes a time before command to fight. Al-Biqāʿī locates the statement in the early Meccan period of pardon and expects authority over others later."}, {"id": "88:22/q09/p2", "position": "No, fighting does not annul the inability to compel inward faith.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports that professing Muslims are left as they are, with lives and property protected except for due rights. Al-Ṭabrisī says jihad is not coercion, and rejection remains outside the Prophet's responsibility. Quṭb says later jihad removed barriers to hearing the message and persecution of converts. Ibn ʿĀshūr says combat followed polytheist aggression and expulsion, so the statement reassures rather than imposes a temporary ban. Kur'an Yolu says the Prophet never forced belief, while punitive action targeted harmful agitators."}]}
{"id": "88:22/q10", "question": "What does the report recited with this verse say about fighting and reckoning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "88:22/q10/p1", "position": "The Prophet was ordered to fight until profession of God's oneness; then life and property are protected except by right, while God judges the account.", "reasons": "Jābir transmits this wording with the verse recitation in al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās, Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī; al-Durr gives the substance.
